qt: to the Commission Tobiasz Bocheński (ECR) Subject:

CBAM has been portrayed as an instrument designed to prevent carbon leakage and level the playing field between producers from the EU and third countries. At the same time, European industrial representatives are increasingly pointing out that the planned extension of CBAM’s scope to downstream product groups may lead to higher operating costs, more red tape and a decline in the competitiveness of businesses operating within the single market. Particular concerns are being raised by companies acting as links in complex European supply chains, which are warning of the risk of rising costs for components and semi-finished products used in manufacturing. This issue is also of significant importance to Poland, which is one of the largest producers of industrial goods in Central and Eastern Europe and a major exporter of steel, aluminium, automotive parts, machinery and household appliances. For many SMEs, additional reporting obligations could mean a significant increase in operating costs. In light of the foregoing: 1.

Has the Commission carried out an impact assessment of the planned extension of CBAM on the competitiveness of SMEs and on the functioning of European supply chains, particularly in countries such as Poland?
Does the Commission have any analyses at its disposal regarding the anticipated increase in administrative and production costs for enterprises covered by the extended scope of CBAM?
Is the Commission considering introducing simplifications or transitional periods for SMEs in order to reduce the risk of losing competitiveness vis-à-vis non-EU producers?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.11.2026) The legislative proposal revising the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)1 was accompanied by an impact assessment2. This impact assessment relied, inter alia, on a consultation of EU stakeholders, including national competent authorities, customs authorities and industry representatives, as well as small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). It assessed the impacts on, inter alia, the competitiveness of the EU economy. The impact assessment established that the reform would entail limited administrative and compliance costs for businesses3. It found limited impact on the EU macro economy, trade and inflation. Further, the impact assessment found that CBAM’s proposed downstream extension would have a moderate impact on the absolute number of SME importers brought into CBAM’s scope, and limited cost increases for these businesses4. The CBAM Regulation already exempts from CBAM obligations companies importing less than a certain single mass-based threshold (currently set at 50 tonnes) on a yearly basis5. Over 90% of companies importing CBAM goods into the EU are exempted, mostly SMEs, while maintaining over 99% of emissions in scope. Looking ahead, the Commission will continue to keep the implementation of CBAM as simple as possible. For example, in the case of downstream goods there will be no markup thereby facilitating the use of default values. The Commission is also providing guidance to stakeholders in the implementation of the CBAM6.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025PC0989. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025SC0988. 3 The impact assessment found a total annual additional compliance cost for EU importers of about EUR 8-43

million, and total annual enforcement cost per authority and country of about EUR 0.05-0.37 million due to CBAM’s proposed downstream extension. 4 The additional number of SME importers due to CBAM’s proposed downstream extension is estimated to be around 3800-3900. 5 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/2083/oj/eng. 6 https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/carbon-border-adjustment-mechanism/cbam-legislation-andguidance_en.
